cards.title: Ordinary eligibility
cards.front: Check the application qualifications together.
cards.rule: An ordinary applicant must be at least 18, be a U.S. citizen or permanent legal resident, read and write English, have the qualifying RI connection, avoid disqualification and demonstrate knowledge.
cards.boundary: A strong training result satisfies only the knowledge issue.
cards.mixup: Do not confuse a customer's identity requirements with the applicant's qualifications.

cards.title: Professional connection exception
cards.front: Identify the credential-based residency exception.
cards.rule: Section 15(c) permits the specified RI bar members and CPAs to apply regardless of residence using professional evidence.
cards.boundary: Follow the current form's credential-document instructions and other applicable requirements.
cards.mixup: An unrelated professional license does not create the listed exception.

cards.title: Original application oath
cards.front: Prepare the oath before submitting the paper file.
cards.rule: The SOS application route requires both form pages, original signatures and an oath before a Rhode Island notary.
cards.boundary: An emailed scan is not the accepted application submission method.
cards.mixup: A training attendance certificate does not execute the application oath.

cards.title: Assessment target
cards.front: Use the public knowledge tool for preparation.
cards.rule: The Department recommends training and an assessment score of at least 80% to support sufficient knowledge.
cards.boundary: Public source review did not establish an item count or time limit for the linked assessment.
cards.mixup: A site practice percentage does not issue a commission.

cards.title: Limited holdover
cards.front: Remember Rhode Island's post-expiration window.
cards.rule: An appointed notary who is not reappointed may continue officiating for 30 days after expiration under section 15(g).
cards.boundary: After the limited period, a pending renewal alone supplies no further authority.
cards.mixup: Do not change the old commission date into a fictional renewed date.

cards.title: Personal dealings
cards.front: Decide whether personal knowledge is genuine.
cards.rule: Personal knowledge requires dealings sufficient to give reasonable certainty of the individual's identity.
cards.boundary: Media recognition and a new introduction do not automatically establish those dealings.
cards.mixup: Recognizing a public face differs from knowing the individual through sufficient dealings.

cards.title: Expired listed credentials
cards.front: Apply the statutory ID timing rule.
cards.rule: A passport, driver's license or government-issued nondriver ID may be current or expired no more than three years before the act.
cards.boundary: The notary still must identify the appearing individual satisfactorily.
cards.mixup: The three-year window does not make a suspicious or mismatched credential conclusive.

cards.title: Other government ID
cards.front: Check the second government-identification category.
cards.rule: Other government ID must be current or within the three-year expiration window, contain a signature or photograph and satisfy the notary.
cards.boundary: The legislature's signature-or-photo language controls this category despite narrower manual wording.
cards.mixup: A private membership card does not become government ID because it has a photo.

cards.title: Sworn identity witness
cards.front: Distinguish identity testimony from introduction.
cards.rule: A credible witness verifies identity on oath or affirmation and must be known to the notary or identified through the listed credentials.
cards.boundary: The witness must actually know the principal and meet the applicable credible-witness safeguards.
cards.mixup: A friend's unsworn greeting does not perform the verification.

cards.title: Additional identity evidence
cards.front: Respond when the presented credential leaves doubts.
cards.rule: The notary may request further information or identification needed to assure identity.
cards.boundary: A listed credential's date alone does not resolve every mismatch or alteration.
cards.mixup: An urgent deadline does not decide whether evidence is satisfactory.

cards.title: Acknowledged execution
cards.front: Focus on the principal's acknowledgment.
cards.rule: An acknowledgment involves the appearing person acknowledging voluntary execution and the notary determining identity and the person's signature.
cards.boundary: An existing signature can be acknowledged through the proper procedure.
cards.mixup: Do not certify that an unseen old signature was witnessed being affixed.

cards.title: Jurat sequence
cards.front: Keep the jurat's distinct elements together.
cards.rule: The Standards' jurat involves appearance, identification, signing in the notary's presence and an oath or affirmation to the document's truthfulness or accuracy.
cards.boundary: The written certificate must describe the vow actually administered.
cards.mixup: A journal signature alone does not supply an oath.

cards.title: Affirmation
cards.front: Offer the legally equivalent nonreligious vow.
cards.rule: An affirmation uses personal honor without invoking a deity and is legally equivalent to an oath.
cards.boundary: The signer still makes a genuine vow under the stated perjury consequences.
cards.mixup: A religious preference does not require abandoning a proper jurat.

cards.title: Observed signature
cards.front: Observe the event a witnessing certificate describes.
cards.rule: Signature witnessing requires the identified principal to appear and sign before the notary.
cards.boundary: The act does not inherently require swearing to the document's contents.
cards.mixup: A prior signature acknowledgment is a different procedure from observing the signing.

cards.title: Scope of attestation
cards.front: Explain what a notarial act establishes.
cards.rule: The notary performs the specified formalities and certifies the facts of that act.
cards.boundary: The notarial office does not authorize independent guarantees of a document's truthfulness, lawfulness or business wisdom.
cards.mixup: A flawless stamp does not insure a transaction's success.

cards.title: Commissioned signature
cards.front: Keep the official name consistent.
cards.rule: Sign the commissioned name consistently and include the official title, expiration date and notary ID as called for by the Standards.
cards.boundary: Optional stamp fields do not remove separate certificate-completion duties.
cards.mixup: The workplace's preferred abbreviation does not redefine the commissioned name.

cards.title: Truthful event details
cards.front: Make the certificate describe the actual performance.
cards.rule: A notary should not execute a certificate containing information known or believed false.
cards.boundary: A printed venue, date or principal name must still be accurate for the act.
cards.mixup: The document's execution date need not be the later acknowledgment date.

cards.title: Completed certificate
cards.front: Finish the necessary facts before official execution.
cards.rule: The Standards prohibit applying an official signature or stamp to an incomplete certificate.
cards.boundary: A narrow attorney-escrow commercial exception has specific conditions and is unsuitable as a universal shortcut.
cards.mixup: The customer's promise to finish blanks later does not establish compliance.

cards.title: Permitted form alternatives
cards.front: Recognize the Standards' certificate-form exceptions.
cards.rule: The SOS sample forms coexist with specified alternative-state, protected printed and established conveyancing forms.
cards.boundary: The alternative wording must still correspond to a lawful act actually performed.
cards.mixup: Using another state's form does not extend an RI notary's territorial authority.

cards.title: Remote association
cards.front: Connect the remote certificate to its record.
cards.rule: A remote certificate must be part of or securely attached to a tangible record, or affixed or logically associated with an electronic record.
cards.boundary: The notary may sign only after the act has been performed.
cards.mixup: A detached electronic file with no record association does not complete this requirement.

cards.title: Eligibility first
cards.front: Classify the original before certifying its reproduction.
cards.rule: The Standards restrict certification of vital and specified public or publicly recordable records available as certified copies from official sources.
cards.boundary: A private holder's ownership of the paper does not change its official-record category.
cards.mixup: Customer consent cannot make a restricted vital record eligible.

cards.title: Whole reproduction
cards.front: Inspect the copy's completeness.
cards.rule: A certifying officer determines that the copy is a full, true and accurate transcription or reproduction.
cards.boundary: Include relevant reverse sides, attachments and pages rather than assuming the first page is enough.
cards.mixup: A file name matching the original does not establish content accuracy.

cards.title: Comparison procedure
cards.front: Make the required copy determination personally.
cards.rule: Copy certification involves copying, supervising the copying or comparing the original and copy and determining accuracy and completeness.
cards.boundary: The notary's certificate must accurately describe the procedure performed.
cards.mixup: The customer's unsupported assurance does not replace the notary's determination.

cards.title: Electronic-to-paper copy
cards.front: Recognize express tangible-copy authority.
cards.rule: A notarial officer may certify that a tangible copy of an electronic record is accurate.
cards.boundary: The authority still requires actual accuracy of the reproduction.
cards.mixup: Printing alone does not transform a document into a certified copy.

cards.title: Authentication purpose
cards.front: Distinguish the copy task from an apostille.
cards.rule: Apostilles and certifications authenticate public officials' signatures, capacities and seals for the applicable foreign-use process.
cards.boundary: The Department of State handles authentication of Rhode Island public officials' signatures.
cards.mixup: Certifying a reproduction does not itself issue an apostille.

cards.title: Personal stamp
cards.front: Keep the tool within the commissioned notary's control.
cards.rule: The stamp is the exclusive property of the notary and may not be used by another person.
cards.boundary: Employer payment does not transfer ownership or the commission.
cards.mixup: A coworker cannot finish a transaction with another notary's stamp.

cards.title: Stamp design
cards.front: Check the ordinary inked stamp before use.
cards.rule: The ordinary stamp is circular or rectangular with an edge border, the exact commissioned name and the words Notary Public and Rhode Island.
cards.boundary: The notary ID and expiration date are optional stamp additions under the Standards.
cards.mixup: An employer logo does not substitute for the required jurisdiction wording.

cards.title: Copyable impression
cards.front: Verify reproduction of the official stamp.
cards.rule: The stamp must be capable of being copied together with the record.
cards.boundary: The manual describes making an embossed seal inked and copyable with a seal highlighter.
cards.mixup: An invisible dry impression can fail the required copying capability.

cards.title: Prior fee quote
cards.front: Disclose the service charge before performing the act.
cards.rule: Traditional and remote fees may not exceed $25 per document or notarization and must be disclosed beforehand.
cards.boundary: The ceiling permits lower charges or free service.
cards.mixup: A charge below the ceiling still requires prior disclosure.

cards.title: Unworkable stamp notice
cards.front: Report compromised or unusable tools promptly.
cards.rule: Immediately notify the Department in writing of loss, theft, damage or another condition making the stamp unworkable, and report recovery or replacement.
cards.boundary: Notifying only the retailer does not notify the commissioning agency.
cards.mixup: Do not postpone a report until renewal.

cards.title: Financial impartiality
cards.front: Screen the notary's own stake.
cards.rule: The Standards restrict a notary who is a party or financially interested in the subject matter, with specified exceptions.
cards.boundary: The notice-only and RI-attorney exceptions require their stated conditions.
cards.mixup: A smaller notarial fee does not eliminate sale proceeds or beneficiary interests.

cards.title: Family restrictions
cards.front: Recognize the listed close relationships.
cards.rule: Spouse, domestic partner, parent, guardian, child and sibling relationships, including specified in-law, step and half relations, are restricted.
cards.boundary: The Standards describe a narrow RI-attorney-prepared-document exception.
cards.mixup: Different surnames do not remove a sibling or parent relationship.

cards.title: Nonlawyer advertising
cards.front: Use the statutory disclosure across advertisement languages.
cards.rule: A non-RI-attorney advertising notarial services must include the prominent statutory or authorized alternative disclaimer in each language used.
cards.boundary: The statute also restricts notario titles for non-RI-attorney notaries.
cards.mixup: A disclaimer cannot authorize the legal or immigration services the commission does not grant.

cards.title: Original records
cards.front: Respect the customer's access to the source record.
cards.rule: Except as otherwise allowed by law, a notary may not withhold access to or possession of the original record provided for notarization.
cards.boundary: An unrelated debt does not create an automatic right to confiscate the record.
cards.mixup: Notarizing does not transfer document ownership to the notary.

cards.title: Disciplinary process
cards.front: Understand consequences without inventing immunity.
cards.rule: Dishonesty, noncompliance and listed integrity failures may support denial, suspension, revocation or other commission conditions.
cards.boundary: Section 16 provides timely notice and hearing and preserves other legal remedies.
cards.mixup: Commission discipline does not automatically settle every civil claim.

cards.title: Traditional journal status
cards.front: Understand the recommended traditional record.
cards.rule: The Standards recommend a permanently bound chronological journal as best practice for traditional acts.
cards.boundary: Electronic and remote procedures have their own recording and digital-record duties.
cards.mixup: Do not turn the traditional recommendation into a claim that remote recordings are optional.

cards.title: Useful journal fields
cards.front: Preserve the details of the actual procedure.
cards.rule: Recommended fields include time, act and document description, principal and witness details, identity evidence, fee and noncompletion circumstances.
cards.boundary: Record what happened accurately instead of manufacturing a completed act.
cards.mixup: A journal entry does not replace the ceremony it records.

cards.title: Sensitive numbers
cards.front: Avoid unnecessary financial identifiers.
cards.rule: The Standards direct notaries not to record Social Security or credit card numbers in the journal.
cards.boundary: Identity evidence may be described without copying these prohibited numbers.
cards.mixup: A desire for a detailed record does not justify collecting every number visible.

cards.title: End-of-term records
cards.front: Plan stamp and journal disposition separately.
cards.rule: The Standards call for disabling stamps and recommend retaining an elected traditional journal and records for seven years after expiration, resignation or revocation.
cards.boundary: Respect the separate statutory ten-year remote-recording requirement.
cards.mixup: Destroying a stamp does not imply destroying the journal with it.

cards.title: Permanent renewal identity
cards.front: Maintain continuity through the renewal file.
cards.rule: The SOS says the notary ID is permanent and the original ID is used even if the commission has expired.
cards.boundary: A timely completed renewal preserves the expiration month and day while changing the year.
cards.mixup: A late application does not create indefinite holdover authority.

cards.title: Capacity assessment
cards.front: Assess the individual rather than relying on a stereotype.
cards.rule: A notarial officer may refuse if unsatisfied about capacity or a knowingly and voluntarily made signature.
cards.boundary: The Standards prohibit refusal solely on listed grounds such as advanced age or disability.
cards.mixup: A disability does not automatically establish incapacity.

cards.title: Reading access
cards.front: Make the text accessible to the signer.
cards.rule: The manual advises reading the document to blind or illiterate signers before the act and documenting the reading as described.
cards.boundary: A nonlawyer may reread the text without providing legal advice through the commission.
cards.mixup: Reading aloud is different from telling the signer what legal choice to make.

cards.title: Language assistance
cards.front: Support effective communication about the record.
cards.rule: The manual permits shared-language communication or an interpreter and recommends an interpreter accuracy oath and certificate notation.
cards.boundary: Oral translation can suffice, while the notary must understand the certificate language.
cards.mixup: A translator does not automatically replace the principal's own willingness or signature.

cards.title: Written communication
cards.front: Use a suitable method with a deaf signer.
cards.rule: When notary and signer are not competent in sign language, the manual recommends written communication and a journal note about the method.
cards.boundary: The ordinary identity and voluntariness requirements still apply.
cards.mixup: Deafness alone is not a proper sole basis for refusal.

cards.title: Directed signing under statute
cards.front: Apply the legislature's assisted-signature route carefully.
cards.rule: Section 8 allows a physically unable person to direct someone other than the notarial officer to sign, with the required explanatory annotation.
cards.boundary: The manual and Standards describe a different notary-assisted process, so unresolved cases need authoritative clarification.
cards.mixup: Do not silently merge conflicting procedures into a made-up universal rule.

cards.title: Approval sequence
cards.front: Establish digital authority before the first session.
cards.rule: An active RI notary obtains approved technology, supplies electronic signature and stamp samples, submits the update and waits for Department confirmation.
cards.boundary: Vendor costs are separate from the no-fee state information update.
cards.mixup: A purchased subscription alone does not authorize electronic or remote acts.

cards.title: Different presence modes
cards.front: Identify how the signer appears.
cards.rule: In-person electronic notarization uses digital records while signer and notary share physical presence, whereas RON uses secure live audiovisual communication.
cards.boundary: The remote notary must be physically in RI and use authorized procedures.
cards.mixup: Using a laptop does not itself make an in-person act remote.

cards.title: Remote identity alternatives
cards.front: Use an authorized route to identify the remote person.
cards.rule: Section 12.1 recognizes personal knowledge, a qualifying credible witness or at least two different types of identity proofing.
cards.boundary: The chosen route does not remove same-record confirmation or recording duties.
cards.mixup: Common provider KBA procedures should not be described as the statute's only identity option.

cards.title: Remote recording custody
cards.front: Arrange durable access to session evidence.
cards.rule: An audiovisual recording must be created and retained by the responsible person or designated repository for at least ten years under the statutory default.
cards.boundary: Changing vendors does not end the required retention period.
cards.mixup: A digital journal entry alone is not the audiovisual recording.

cards.title: Foreign-location safeguards
cards.front: Check additional conditions for signers abroad.
cards.rule: For a signer outside the United States, section 12.1 requires the specified U.S.-connected record and that signing or making the statement is not prohibited in the foreign state.
cards.boundary: The Standards and guide use broader outside-RI wording, so this material avoids resolving intermediate-location conflicts.
cards.mixup: An overseas location is not an automatic permission for every foreign transaction.

appointment.summary: Follow Rhode Island's knowledge-based commission route from qualifications through the original application oath, issuance and renewal. Treat education, appointment and digital authorization as distinct steps.

sections.heading: Qualify and prepare before filing
sections.body: Section 42-30.1-15 requires the ordinary applicant to be at least 18, be a U.S. citizen or permanent legal resident, read and write English, have Rhode Island residence, employment or practice, avoid disqualification and demonstrate sufficient knowledge. The Department recommends its free training and Knowledge Assessment with an 80% target. The public linked entry did not establish the assessment's question count or time limit. RI bar members and specified CPAs have a professional-credential route regardless of residence. Use the current application instructions for their required evidence.

sections.heading: Original oath, fee and ongoing authority
sections.body: The first-commission and renewal pages direct applicants to complete both pages with original signatures, appear before a Rhode Island notary for the oath and submit the ordinary $80 fee with the application by mail or in person. The Department rejects email applications. The ordinary commission term is four years. Section 15(g) permits an unreappointed notary to officiate for 30 days after expiration, and the renewal page repeats that limited holdover. Beyond it, await reappointment before acting. Official basis checked November 14, 2026, section 15, the April 2025 application form and the SOS application and renewal pages.

example.heading: Worked example — the late renewal
example.body: A notary discovers that the commission expired six weeks earlier and mails a complete renewal. The old notary ID remains permanent, but six weeks exceeds the statutory 30-day holdover. Mailing the renewal does not immediately restore authority. The notary arranges another properly authorized notary for the pending customer and waits for reappointment.

keyFacts: The ordinary commission lasts four years and the ordinary filing fee is $80.
The Department recommends an 80% Knowledge Assessment target.
The statutory post-expiration holdover is limited to 30 days.

identity.summary: Establish who appears through sufficient personal dealings, qualifying government identification or a properly sworn credible witness. Keep identity separate from appearance and willingness.

sections.heading: Apply the legislature's identity categories
sections.body: Section 42-30.1-6 recognizes personal knowledge based on dealings sufficient to provide reasonable certainty of identity. It also lists a passport, driver's license or government-issued nondriver ID current or expired no more than three years. Another government identification category uses the same timing limit, requires a signature or photograph and must satisfy the notary. The manual's identification discussion contains narrower language, so this chapter uses the statutory text for the expiration and signature-or-photograph questions. Copies, private memberships and a confident introduction do not automatically supply a listed identity method.

sections.heading: Witnesses, doubts and the current appearance
sections.body: A credible witness verifies identity through oath or affirmation and must be known to the notary or identified by the specified credentials. The Standards describe honesty, reliability and impartiality, with personal knowledge of the principal. Section 6(c) permits further information or credentials when needed to assure identity. Even satisfactory ID does not replace the current personal appearance required by section 5, the actual requested act or the capacity and willingness assessment. Official basis checked November 14, 2026, sections 5 and 6 and Standards section 2.

example.heading: Worked example — a clear license with a mismatch
example.body: A customer presents a driver's license expired two years ago, but the photograph does not resemble the person at the desk. The expiration falls within the statutory three-year window. The mismatch still prevents treating the document as conclusive. The notary requests additional appropriate evidence under section 6(c) and proceeds only if the person is satisfactorily identified.

keyFacts: Listed IDs may be current or expired no more than three years.
Other government ID under section 6(b)(1)(ii) requires a signature or photograph.
A credible witness supplies identity verification on oath or affirmation.

acts.summary: Choose the procedure the customer actually needs and perform each of its elements. Rhode Island distinguishes acknowledgment, jurat, standalone oath or affirmation, signature witnessing and copy certification.

sections.heading: Voluntary acknowledgment and witnessed signing
sections.body: For an acknowledgment, section 42-30.1-4(a) requires the notary to determine the appearing person's identity and that the signature is theirs. The manual describes acknowledging that execution was competent and voluntary, including representative capacity when applicable. An already affixed signature can be acknowledged through the proper procedure. Signature witnessing instead requires the identified person to sign in the notary's presence. Its certificate describes the observed signing event. A notary who sees an old signature cannot truthfully claim to have witnessed its earlier affixation.

sections.heading: Truthfulness vows and completion
sections.body: The Standards define a jurat through appearance, identification, signing before the notary and an oath or affirmation vouching for the signed document's truthfulness or accuracy. An affirmation is legally equivalent to an oath and uses personal honor without a religious invocation. Printed words on an affidavit do not administer the vow. Complete the corresponding certificate with facts matching the actual procedure, and distinguish a standalone oral oath from a certificate-based document act. Official basis checked November 14, 2026, section 4, Standards section 2 and manual pages 10-13.

example.heading: Worked example — the wrong certificate
example.body: A customer asks for a jurat on a statement signed at home and says there is no time for an oath. The notary explains that the requested jurat requires signing before the notary and a genuine oath or affirmation. Applying an acknowledgment certificate just to avoid those steps would change the requested act. The customer obtains instructions about the needed act and returns for the proper procedure.

keyFacts: An acknowledgment may address an existing signature through the proper acknowledgment.
A jurat includes an oath or affirmation and signing before the notary.
Signature witnessing observes signing and does not inherently include a truthfulness oath.

certificates.summary: Make every official certificate describe the notarial event truthfully. Check the principal, venue, date, act, commissioned signature and required commission details before execution.

sections.heading: Truthful, complete official statements
sections.body: Standards section 3(b) calls for the commissioned signature, official title, commission expiration and notary identification number. Section 4 prohibits false certificate information and signing or stamping an incomplete certificate. Preprinted facts require the same care as handwritten entries. An acknowledgment performed today takes today's actual acknowledgment facts even if the underlying document was signed earlier. A document's destination does not determine where the notary actually performs the act. Do not send an ordinary consumer a signed blank certificate for later completion or attachment.

sections.heading: Form choices and remote record association
sections.body: The Standards recognize specified alternative-state certificates, printed forms that prohibit alteration and established conveyancing forms. Their sample certificates do not erase those stated exceptions. A narrow commercial non-consumer attorney-escrow exception has several conditions and does not authorize false facts. For remote certificates, section 42-30.1-12.2 requires contemporaneous execution, signature and date, jurisdiction, title and applicable expiration. The act must be performed before the notary signs. Connect the certificate securely to a tangible record or logically associate it with an electronic record. Official basis checked November 14, 2026, Standards sections 3-4 and section 12.2.

example.heading: Worked example — an incorrect printed venue
example.body: A customer brings a form printed for another state, and the certificate lists that state's county. The lawful act is performed in Providence. The notary checks the permitted form and makes sure the certificate truthfully identifies the actual venue and procedure. Retaining a false printed location merely because it arrived on the form would not satisfy truthful certification.

keyFacts: A preprinted certificate still needs accurate event facts.
Do not sign or stamp an incomplete certificate.
A remote certificate must remain connected to the record it certifies.

copies.summary: Classify the original, verify the whole reproduction and use the appropriate certificate. Official-record custodians and apostille services perform different functions from an ordinary notarial copy certification.

sections.heading: Record category and faithful reproduction
sections.body: Standards sections 2(c) and 4(a)(1) exclude vital records and specified public or publicly recordable records available as certified copies from official sources. Direct a birth, marriage or death certificate request to the proper custodian. A customer's possession of the original does not change its official category. For an eligible record, the notary copies, supervises copying or compares the copy, then determines accuracy and completeness. Section 42-30.1-4(d) requires a full, true and accurate reproduction. Inspect reverse sides, attachments and page sequence.

sections.heading: Electronic sources and foreign-use authentication
sections.body: Section 42-30.1-3(b) expressly permits certifying that a tangible copy accurately reproduces an electronic record. That authority requires actual accuracy. Copy certification does not prove the author's claims, guarantee enforceability or issue an apostille. The manual identifies the Department of State as the office authenticating Rhode Island public officials' signatures for applicable apostille or certification processes. Determine what the receiving authority actually requests before treating a simple copy certificate as sufficient. Official basis checked November 14, 2026, sections 3-4, Standards sections 2-4 and manual pages 14 and 21.

example.heading: Worked example — two different requests
example.body: A customer presents a birth certificate and a private letter, asking for certified copies of both. The notary refers the vital-record request to the official custodian. The private letter can be evaluated under the eligible-copy procedure. Its reverse-side notes must be reproduced and compared before the notary can truthfully certify a complete copy.

keyFacts: Check official-record exclusions before copying.
Certify only a full, true and accurate reproduction.
An apostille authenticates an official signature through a separate process.

tools-fees.summary: Use a personal, compliant and copyable stamp. Quote lawful fees before performing the service and protect the commission's tools even when an employer paid for them.

sections.heading: Required stamp and personal custody
sections.body: The SOS and Standards prescribe an inked circular or rectangular stamp with an edge border, the exact commissioned name and the words Notary Public and Rhode Island. The notary ID and expiration may be added to the stamp, while certificate-completion duties are separate. Section 42-30.1-13 requires the stamp to be copyable with the record. The manual explains how an embosser can be made inked and copyable with a highlighter. The stamp belongs exclusively to the notary and cannot be used by a coworker. Employer payment does not transfer that ownership.

sections.heading: Fee ceiling and prompt tool reports
sections.body: Section 42-30.1-20.1 sets a $25 maximum per document or notarization for traditional and remote acts and requires prior disclosure to the service user. The notary may charge less or work free. Disclosure after completion remains too late even if the amount is below the ceiling. Standards section 5 calls for immediate written notice to the Department when a stamp is lost, stolen, damaged or otherwise unworkable, followed by notice of recovery or replacement. Official basis checked November 14, 2026, sections 13 and 20.1, Standards sections 3 and 5 and manual pages 7 and 18.

example.heading: Worked example — employer-paid tools
example.body: A bank buys a stamp for its commissioned employee and later asks a receptionist to use it while the notary is absent. The employee must retain control. The bank's purchase did not commission the receptionist or transfer the stamp's exclusive use. The customer needs a properly authorized notary to perform the complete act.

keyFacts: The ordinary stamp needs an edge border and the required name and state wording.
The notarial fee ceiling is $25 per document or notarization with advance disclosure.
Report a lost, stolen or unworkable stamp immediately in writing.

conduct.summary: Preserve impartiality, respect the limits of the commission and make truthful representations about notarial services. Separate conflicts and advertising duties from the mechanics of stamping.

sections.heading: Financial and relationship conflicts
sections.body: Standards section 4 restricts notarizing as a party, named person or financially interested participant, subject to stated exceptions. It also lists spouse, domestic partner, parent, guardian, child and sibling relationships including specified in-law, step and half relatives. The Standards include narrow notice-only and RI-attorney-related exceptions. Apply their actual conditions. A different surname, no notarial fee or a customer's consent does not automatically remove a prohibited relationship or financial stake. Employment does not relieve a notary from screening the real transaction.

sections.heading: Public representations and consequences
sections.body: Section 42-30.1-18 does not grant legal-drafting, legal-advice or immigration-representation powers through a notary commission. Non-RI-attorney notaries must avoid the restricted notario titles and follow the prominent multilingual advertising disclaimer rule. Except as otherwise allowed by law, do not withhold the customer's original record. Section 16 permits discipline for dishonest applications, noncompliance and listed integrity failures while providing notice and hearing and preserving other remedies. Official basis checked November 14, 2026, sections 16 and 18 and Standards section 4.

example.heading: Worked example — two sources of conflict
example.body: A nonattorney notary is asked to acknowledge a sibling's signature on a business sale that also pays the notary a share of the proceeds. The family relationship and financial interest each require examination under the Standards. Waiving the small notarial fee would not remove either issue. The parties arrange an impartial notary outside those conflicts.

keyFacts: Listed close-family and financial interests trigger the Standards' restrictions.
A commission does not license legal or immigration advice.
Nonattorney advertising requires the applicable prominent disclaimer in each language used.

records.summary: Maintain an accurate commission file and useful records of notarial acts. Distinguish the recommended traditional journal, end-of-term practices and mandatory remote recording retention.

sections.heading: Document the actual ceremony
sections.body: Standards section 3(e) recommends a permanently bound chronological journal for traditional acts. Recommended details include date and time, act and document description, principal and witness information, identity evidence, fee and reasons for noncompletion. Do not record Social Security or credit card numbers. A journal should record the procedure that actually occurred and distinguish principal from witness. It cannot establish an appearance, oath or signature that never occurred. Digital and remote acts have additional record and recording duties under their governing authorities.

sections.heading: Update, renew and conclude the commission
sections.body: Standards section 5 calls for residence and name changes to be reported within ten days. The SOS says the notary ID is permanent and should be reused for renewal, even following expiration. Timely completed renewals preserve the expiration month and day. If qualifications end, address resignation and written notice. Section 7 calls for stamps to be disabled and recommends retaining an elected traditional journal for seven years after expiration, resignation or revocation. Section 12.1 separately requires the default ten-year remote recording retention. Official basis checked November 14, 2026, Standards sections 3 and 5-7, the renewal page and section 12.1.

example.heading: Worked example — a refused request
example.body: A customer appears with unreliable identification and the notary cannot resolve the mismatch. The notary declines to complete the act and, in the elected traditional journal, records the date, requested act, actual evidence and reason for noncompletion. The entry does not falsely claim that an acknowledgment was completed and excludes Social Security or credit card numbers.

keyFacts: The traditional journal is recommended best practice.
Do not record Social Security or credit card numbers.
Keep the seven-year traditional-journal recommendation distinct from the ten-year remote-recording requirement.

access.summary: Provide an effective way for the principal to understand and participate. Consider capacity and voluntariness individually while following the official guidance for reading, translation and assisted signing.

sections.heading: Accessible communication and individual assessment
sections.body: The manual recommends reading the document to blind or illiterate signers, allowing rereading and documenting the assistance as described. A nonlawyer's reading does not become authority for legal advice. For a deaf signer, use competent sign language or the recommended written communication. For a signer who does not speak the notary's language, the manual permits an interpreter and oral translation, with a recommended accuracy oath and certificate notation. The notary must understand the certificate language and still assess identity, comprehension and free will. The Standards prohibit refusal solely on listed grounds such as disability or advanced age.

sections.heading: Representative and directed-signature boundaries
sections.body: The manual recommends obtaining a power-of-attorney copy and noting an appearing attorney-in-fact's representative capacity. A representative's identity must be distinguished from the absent principal's identity. Section 42-30.1-8 permits a physically unable person to direct another individual other than the notarial officer to sign and requires an explanatory annotation. The manual and Standards describe a different notary-assisted route. This chapter uses the statute's express route and preserves that unresolved conflict for authoritative clarification. Official basis checked November 14, 2026, sections 7-8, Standards section 4 and manual pages 15-16.

example.heading: Worked example — written participation
example.body: A deaf signer and the notary do not share competent sign language. They communicate in writing about the requested act and the signer's willingness. The notary checks identity and capacity under the ordinary requirements and notes the communication method in the elected journal. The signer participates personally, and a companion is not treated as automatically speaking or signing for them.

keyFacts: Disability and advanced age alone do not establish incapacity.
Use communication the principal and notary can actually understand.
Section 8's directed signer is someone other than the notarial officer.

digital.summary: Build electronic and remote capability on an active Rhode Island commission. Use approved technology and the required identity, record, certificate and retention safeguards for each session.

sections.heading: Authorization and presence mode
sections.body: The SOS requires a current RI commission, approved solution-provider services, electronic signature and stamp samples and the information update, with Department confirmation before digital notarization begins. The update has no state filing fee, while providers charge for services. Complete provider training. In-person electronic notarization retains shared physical presence with digital records and signatures. RON uses secure simultaneous audiovisual communication, and the notary must be physically in Rhode Island. An ordinary Zoom or FaceTime call does not establish an approved procedure.

sections.heading: Remote identity, record integrity and retention
sections.body: Section 42-30.1-12.1 recognizes personal knowledge, a qualifying credible witness or at least two identity-proofing types. Confirm that the notary and signer refer to the same record, create an audiovisual recording and retain it for at least ten years under the statutory default. The remote certificate must indicate use of communication technology. A signer outside the United States triggers the statutory U.S.-connection and foreign-permission safeguards. The Standards and guide have broader outside-RI wording and legacy paper procedures, so uncertain edge cases require clarification. Official basis checked November 14, 2026, sections 12.1-14 and the SOS digital pages.

example.heading: Worked example — traveling with a subscription
example.body: An approved RI remote notary visits Connecticut and receives an urgent request from a Rhode Island customer. The customer, record and vendor account are ready, but the notary's actual location is outside RI. The notary cannot perform that RI remote act from Connecticut. The parties arrange a properly located authorized notary or reschedule after the notary returns.

keyFacts: Wait for Department confirmation before digital acts.
The remote notary must be physically in Rhode Island.
The statutory default for audiovisual recordings is at least ten years.

articles.intent: Choose and perform the requested signature procedure
articles.title: Rhode Island Acknowledgments, Jurats and the Signature Already on the Page
articles.description: Understand how a previously signed record, an oath and observed signing change a Rhode Island notary's procedure.
articles.h1: The signature is already there. What act is required?
articles.lede: The presence of a signature does not tell an RI notary which ceremony to perform. Start with the requested act and the certificate, then apply its requirements to the person who appears.

sections.heading: Acknowledge an existing execution
sections.body: An acknowledgment can address a signature placed on the record before the appointment. Section 42-30.1-4(a) requires the notary to determine the appearing individual's identity and that the signature is theirs. The official manual also describes the person's acknowledgment of competent and voluntary execution. The certificate records today's acknowledgment event. It should not falsely imply that the notary watched last week's signing.

sections.heading: Administer the jurat's actual vow
sections.body: A jurat adds requirements the mere existence of ink cannot satisfy. Standards section 2(g) includes signing before the notary and taking an oath or affirmation vouching for truthfulness or accuracy. A statement printed above a signature line does not administer that vow. A signer may affirm on personal honor instead of using religious language. The Standards give the affirmation legal equivalence to the oath.

sections.heading: Witness the signing when that is the requested act
sections.body: Signature witnessing concerns an identified person signing in the notary's presence and does not inherently require a truthfulness oath. It therefore differs both from acknowledging a prior signature and from a jurat. If the customer has a completed signature but requests a witnessed-signing certificate, the notary must arrange a procedure that truthfully satisfies the requested act rather than describe an unseen earlier event as witnessed.

sections.heading: Match the certificate to what occurred
sections.body: Suppose a customer brings a pre-signed sworn statement and asks the notary to skip the oath because the office is closing. A notary cannot complete a jurat based only on identity and a stamp. The required signing and vow must occur. Replacing the jurat with an acknowledgment solely to shorten the appointment would change the requested act. Resolve which act the receiving party requires and then complete the corresponding truthful certificate.

faqs.q: Can an acknowledgment involve a signature made earlier?
faqs.a: Yes, if the signer appears, is properly identified and makes the required acknowledgment of that signature.

faqs.q: Can an affirmation support a jurat?
faqs.a: Yes. The Standards recognize an affirmation as legally equivalent to an oath.

articles.intent: Apply statutory identity categories to imperfect evidence
articles.title: Rhode Island Expired ID and the Notary's Remaining Identity Questions
articles.description: Apply the three-year statutory ID window while evaluating mismatches, credible witnesses and additional evidence.
articles.h1: An ID can be within the window and still leave a question
articles.lede: Rhode Island's current identity statute permits specified expired credentials within a limited window. The notary still needs reasonable certainty about the person who appears.

sections.heading: Use the current statutory categories
sections.body: Section 42-30.1-6(b)(1)(i) lists a passport, driver's license or government-issued nondriver ID that is current or expired no more than three years before the act. The date is measured against performance of the notarial act. A four-year-expired passport falls outside that listed window. A two-year-expired driver's license is within the timing category, subject to the other necessary identity determinations.

sections.heading: Read the second category precisely
sections.body: Other government identification under section 6(b)(1)(ii) must fit the same expiration window, contain a signature or photograph and be satisfactory to the officer. The manual uses some narrower wording about photographs and signatures. For these statutory distinctions, read the legislature's text directly. A privately issued gym or employee card does not become government identification merely by carrying an attractive photograph.

sections.heading: Respond to a mismatch
sections.body: A card's acceptable expiration date does not settle a photograph mismatch, apparent alteration or uncertainty about who is presenting it. Section 6(c) authorizes additional information or credentials necessary to assure identity. Pause and evaluate that evidence. Charging more, writing a detailed journal entry or obtaining the customer's consent does not turn unresolved identity evidence into a satisfactory determination.

sections.heading: Use personal knowledge or a witness appropriately
sections.body: Personal knowledge comes from sufficient dealings, not simply recognizing a face from television. A credible witness verifies identity on oath or affirmation and must be known to the notary or identified through the specified credentials. The Standards also describe the witness as honest, reliable and impartial. Record the identity route actually used when keeping a journal, and retain the separate appearance and willingness requirements.

faqs.q: Does Rhode Island reject every expired driver's license?
faqs.a: No. Section 6 permits the listed credential if current or expired no more than three years, subject to satisfactory identification.

faqs.q: May the notary request additional evidence?
faqs.a: Yes. Section 6(c) authorizes additional information or identification needed to assure identity.

articles.intent: Set and communicate lawful notarial fees
articles.title: Quoting Rhode Island Notary Fees Before the Appointment Is Complete
articles.description: Understand the $25 notarial fee ceiling, prior disclosure and the distinction between state filing and vendor charges.
articles.h1: Give the fee information before performing the act
articles.lede: A lawful amount and timely disclosure are separate parts of Rhode Island's fee rule. Even a modest charge must be disclosed before the notarial act.

sections.heading: Start with the service being charged
sections.body: Section 42-30.1-20.1(a) permits a notarial fee up to $25 per document or notarization. Subsection (b) applies the same ceiling to a remote act. The statutory wording does not require every notary to charge the maximum. A notary may charge less or provide a free act. Avoid inventing a per-page formula or an unlimited fee simply because a customer has consented to pay.

sections.heading: Disclose the amount beforehand
sections.body: The statute requires all fees to be disclosed to the person using the service before performance. A customer who hears the price only after the completed certificate has been handed over did not receive that prior disclosure. A workplace's internal price list can help staff quote consistently, but a secret list does not itself communicate the amount to the person being served.

sections.heading: Keep different charges understandable
sections.body: The ordinary $80 commission application fee is paid in the appointment process and is distinct from a customer's notarial-act fee. The SOS remote-authority information update carries no state filing fee, while solution providers can charge for subscriptions. A notary preparing a service quote should identify the actual charge and the applicable authority instead of combining unrelated amounts into an unexplained claim about a state-required customer fee.

sections.heading: Apply the rule to an office interaction
sections.body: A customer arrives for a single ordinary notarization. The employee quotes $10 before the procedure, then the notary screens identity, willingness and the required act. That quote is within the statutory ceiling and timely. A $40 notarial fee for that same single document/notarization would exceed the ceiling even if the customer agreed. A $10 amount first revealed after completion would still miss the timing requirement.

faqs.q: Must an RI notary charge exactly $25?
faqs.a: No. The statute permits a fee up to that ceiling.

faqs.q: Does remote notarization have a separate unlimited fee?
faqs.a: No. Section 20.1(b) also imposes the $25 ceiling and prior disclosure for remote acts.

articles.keyword: Rhode Island employer notary stamp ownership
articles.intent: Maintain personal control of workplace notary tools
articles.title: Who Controls an Employer-Paid Rhode Island Notary Stamp?
articles.description: Review personal stamp ownership, coworker use, compliant design and immediate loss reporting in an office setting.
articles.h1: Employer payment does not transfer the notarial tool
articles.lede: An office may pay for its employee's commission and supplies. The individual notary still controls the stamp and is responsible for the act it authenticates.

sections.heading: The commission remains personal
sections.body: The manual explains that the notary owns the commission, stamp and journal regardless of employer payment. Standards section 3(d) makes the stamp the notary's exclusive property and prohibits use by another person. A receptionist cannot borrow it to complete an absent employee's appointment. The office should arrange another commissioned notary who will perform the entire required procedure under their own authority.

sections.heading: Check the tool before using it
sections.body: The ordinary stamp must be circular or rectangular with an edge border, the exact commissioned name and the words Notary Public and Rhode Island. The SOS calls for an inked stamp. Notary ID and expiration date may be included on the stamp, but certificate completion has separate requirements. If the stamp contains an outdated expiration after renewal, the renewal page directs the notary to order a new stamp.

sections.heading: Protect a usable impression
sections.body: Section 42-30.1-13 requires copying capability together with the record. A dry embossed impression that disappears when scanned can cause a problem. The manual describes using an inked seal highlighter with an embosser. The official impression must remain intelligible, and the tool must remain controlled by its commissioned owner. An unlocked communal drawer makes unauthorized use easier and does not change the exclusive-use rule.

sections.heading: Handle loss and departure promptly
sections.body: Standards section 5 calls for immediate written Department notice when a stamp is lost, stolen, damaged or otherwise unworkable, and notice when it is recovered or replaced. A report to the retailer alone does not reach the commissioning agency. When employment ends, the notary should retain the personal tools rather than surrender them for a replacement employee's use. End-of-commission disposition is governed separately by section 7.

faqs.q: Can an employer keep the stamp because it paid the invoice?
faqs.a: The manual states that ownership and control remain with the individual notary.

faqs.q: Who receives notice of a stolen stamp?
faqs.a: The Standards call for immediate written notice to the Rhode Island Department of State.

articles.keyword: Rhode Island copy certification vital records
articles.intent: Evaluate which certified-copy service is appropriate
articles.title: Rhode Island Copy Requests, Vital Records and the Official Custodian
articles.description: Screen a copy-certification request for official-record exclusions and verify an eligible reproduction accurately.
articles.h1: Classify the original before making a certified copy
articles.lede: Two papers in the same customer's folder may require different certified-copy routes. Record type and the source of official copies matter before the notary reaches for the copier.

sections.heading: Identify records with official sources
sections.body: Standards sections 2(c) and 4(a)(1) restrict notarial copy certification of vital records and specified public or publicly recordable records available from official certified-copy sources. A birth, marriage or death certificate belongs in that official-record inquiry. The customer holding the original does not change its character. Direct the request to the proper custodian instead of promising that a private stamp will substitute for the official certification.

sections.heading: Verify every relevant part of an eligible original
sections.body: For an eligible private record, determine that the reproduction is full, true and accurate under section 42-30.1-4(d). Compare pages, relevant reverse sides and attachments. A scanner can clip signatures, omit a schedule or rearrange pages while keeping a convincing file name. The notary must perform the applicable copying, supervision or comparison and make the determination, rather than simply repeat the customer's unsupported assurance.

sections.heading: Handle an electronic source
sections.body: Section 42-30.1-3(b) expressly authorizes certification of an accurate tangible copy of an electronic record. This is useful when a customer needs a paper reproduction, but printing is only the mechanical step. The officer still checks accuracy. A paper copy containing an altered paragraph cannot be truthfully certified as the accurate electronic-to-paper reproduction the statute describes.

sections.heading: Ask what the recipient needs
sections.body: A copy certificate establishes the eligible reproduction's accuracy. It does not guarantee the author's factual assertions, the agreement's legal enforceability or acceptance by a foreign authority. An apostille or certification authenticating a public official's signature is a different service handled by the Department of State for RI public officials. Clarify the requested service so a customer is directed to the office that can actually supply it.

faqs.q: May a customer waive the birth-certificate restriction?
faqs.a: Customer consent does not expand the notary's copy-certification authority.

faqs.q: Can an accurate paper copy of an electronic record be certified?
faqs.a: Section 3(b) expressly recognizes that authority, subject to actual accuracy and other applicable limits.

articles.keyword: Rhode Island notary interpreter deaf blind signer
articles.intent: Provide accessible communication within notarial scope
articles.title: Reading, Translation and Written Communication for Rhode Island Signers
articles.description: Use official guidance to support blind, deaf, illiterate and non-English-speaking signers while preserving personal participation.
articles.h1: Give the principal a way to understand and participate
articles.lede: Rhode Island's manual offers practical communication methods for several signing circumstances. Accessibility and the ordinary notarial safeguards operate together.

sections.heading: Read when the principal needs reading access
sections.body: For a blind or illiterate signer, the manual advises reading the document before the act and documenting that assistance as described. A signer may ask for part of the text to be read again. The nonlawyer notary can reread without using the commission to advise which legal choice the signer should make. Reading the text does not establish a law license or turn the notary into the customer's legal representative.

sections.heading: Communicate with a deaf signer
sections.body: When notary and signer are not competent in sign language, the manual recommends written communication and a note in the journal describing the method. Use that communication to address the requested act and the principal's participation. A companion's presence does not automatically authorize the companion to answer or sign in place of the principal. Continue to identify the actual signer and assess willingness and capacity.

sections.heading: Use language assistance transparently
sections.body: The manual allows a shared language between signer and notary or use of an interpreter. An oral translation can be sufficient. The guidance strongly suggests administering an interpreter oath or affirmation about accuracy and noting the translator in the certificate. The notary must be able to read and write the certificate's language even where the underlying document is in another language.

sections.heading: Assess the individual circumstances
sections.body: Standards section 4(b) prohibits refusal solely on listed grounds such as advanced age, national origin, health or disability. Section 42-30.1-7 allows refusal where the officer is unsatisfied about capacity or knowingly and voluntarily made signing. These standards require attention to the individual. Neither a disability stereotype nor an unexplained nod resolves the principal's comprehension. Use effective communication to evaluate the actual act.

faqs.q: Does the manual always require a written translation?
faqs.a: No. It states that an oral translation can be sufficient.

faqs.q: Does blindness itself establish incapacity?
faqs.a: No. Provide the described reading access and assess the person's actual capacity and willingness.

articles.keyword: Rhode Island notary family financial interest
articles.intent: Screen and understand conflicts under the Standards
articles.title: Rhode Island Family and Financial Conflicts Before Stamping
articles.description: Evaluate listed relationships, personal transaction interests and narrow exceptions without treating consent as a universal waiver.
articles.h1: Screen the notary's role as well as the signer's identity
articles.lede: A perfectly identified customer can still present a conflict for a particular notary. Rhode Island's Standards address personal interests and close relationships before the mechanics of certification.

sections.heading: Look for a direct transaction interest
sections.body: Section 4(a) restricts acting as a party or named person and addresses financial interests in the subject matter or direct consideration beyond the allowed notarial fees. A seller receiving sale proceeds has a different stake from simply charging the ordinary notarial fee. Reducing the fee to zero does not remove proceeds, property interests or another personal benefit from the transaction.

sections.heading: Check the listed relationships
sections.body: The Standards list spouse, domestic partner, parent, guardian, child and sibling relationships, including specified in-law, step and half relatives. A different surname does not erase a sibling relationship. The family restriction is not written as a rule that applies only when a fee is charged. When the ordinary restriction applies, use an impartial notary who can perform the requested act without the relationship conflict.

sections.heading: Read exceptions as written
sections.body: The named-person restriction has a notice-recipient-only exception. The Standards also contain specified RI-attorney-related fiduciary and fee exceptions and a narrow provision involving relatives witnessing documents prepared by an RI attorney notary. Those details matter. Being a professional in an unrelated field or using an attorney's stationery does not automatically fit them. Apply the actual conditions before relying on an exception.

sections.heading: Preserve the rest of the procedure
sections.body: An exception to a conflict restriction does not create an exception to identification, willingness, the required oath or truthful certificate facts. For example, a notary listed solely to receive notices still needs the principal's proper appearance and acknowledgment. A workplace supervisor's approval does not make a false date true. Keep the conflict inquiry and the act's required formalities in the same complete workflow.

faqs.q: Does waiving the notarial fee remove a financial interest in sale proceeds?
faqs.a: No. The separate stake in the transaction remains relevant under the Standards.

faqs.q: Do different surnames remove a sibling conflict?
faqs.a: No. The provision addresses the actual relationship.

articles.keyword: Rhode Island remote notary recording retention
articles.intent: Understand remote evidence and record-integrity obligations
articles.title: Rhode Island RON Recordings, Same-Record Checks and Long-Term Custody
articles.description: Plan for the remote recording, ten-year default retention and the certificate's link to the executed record.
articles.h1: Plan the evidence before starting the remote session
articles.lede: A completed remote act leaves more than a signed file. Rhode Island law requires an audiovisual record and ties the certificate to the actual record on which the signer acted.

sections.heading: Confirm authority and physical location
sections.body: The SOS requires a current RI commission, approved technology, electronic signature and stamp samples and Department confirmation before digital acts. The remote notary must be physically in Rhode Island. A paid vendor account does not independently authorize the procedure, and a personal video meeting is not the approved-provider route. Complete the chosen provider's training before conducting sessions.

sections.heading: Keep signer and record aligned
sections.body: Section 42-30.1-12.1(b)(2) requires reasonable ability to confirm that the record before the notary is the same one on which the remote person made a statement or executed a signature. A screen-share showing a similar draft does not resolve a mismatch. Use the authorized system's process to establish the actual record, and stop if the necessary confirmation cannot be made.

sections.heading: Arrange the recording's custody
sections.body: The notary or someone acting on the notary's behalf must create an audiovisual recording of performance. Section 12.1(e) permits retention through the responsible person or a designated repository and sets a default minimum of ten years unless a different period is required by rule. Changing subscriptions, employers or providers does not turn a ten-year obligation into a one-year obligation. Preserve access through those transitions.

sections.heading: Complete and associate the certificate
sections.body: The remote certificate must indicate use of communication technology. Section 12.2 prohibits signing before the act has occurred and requires a certificate that is connected to the tangible record or logically associated with the electronic record. A journal entry and a video recording serve different functions and neither replaces a truthful certificate. Plan these components as parts of one complete remote procedure.

faqs.q: What is the default remote-recording retention period?
faqs.a: At least ten years after creation unless a different period is required by applicable rule.

faqs.q: Does a digital journal replace the audiovisual recording?
faqs.a: No. The recording is a separate statutory requirement for the remote act.

articles.keyword: Rhode Island notary advertising disclaimer notario
articles.intent: Advertise within the statutory authority and disclosure rules
articles.title: Advertising Rhode Island Notarial Services Without Overstating Authority
articles.description: Understand the nonattorney disclaimer, multilingual advertising and the limits on notario and immigration-service representations.
articles.h1: Describe the service the commission actually authorizes
articles.lede: A notary's public description of their services is part of professional compliance. Rhode Island law addresses both misleading claims and specific nonattorney disclosures.

sections.heading: Avoid promising legal powers through the commission
sections.body: Section 42-30.1-18(a) states that the commission does not authorize legal drafting, legal advice, immigration consulting or immigration-related representation. A course certificate or years of stamping experience does not add those powers to the commission. Avoid suggesting that an ordinary acknowledgment includes a legal review of the transaction or guarantees approval by a court or immigration agency.

sections.heading: Use the nonattorney disclosure
sections.body: Section 18(d) requires an RI notary who is not an attorney licensed in the state and advertises notarial services to include the statutory or authorized alternative statement prominently. Its substance identifies the lack of an RI attorney license and authority to draft legal records, advise on legal matters including immigration or charge for those activities. The statute gives the exact wording and should be consulted when preparing the advertisement.

sections.heading: Apply the language and media rules
sections.body: The disclaimer must appear in each language used in the advertisement or representation. A bilingual web page therefore needs the required disclosure in both languages. The size-related alternative in section 18(d) concerns the specified nonbroadcast, nonprint and noninternet form that cannot fit the statement. It permits prominent display or provision at the place of performance before the act, rather than a universal omission for small advertisements.

sections.heading: Check titles and claims
sections.body: Section 18(c) prohibits the terms notario or notario publico for a notary who is not an RI-licensed attorney. Translating the title does not expand the office into a civil-law legal profession. Section 18(b) also prohibits false or deceptive advertising. Before publishing a service description, check the titles, promised services, disclaimer language and any claimed guarantee against the actual authority conferred by law.

faqs.q: Can a nonlawyer use notario publico as a marketing title?
faqs.a: Section 18(c) prohibits that term for a notary who is not an RI-licensed attorney.

faqs.q: Does an English disclaimer cover every language in an advertisement?
faqs.a: The statute requires the disclosure in each language used.

articles.keyword: Rhode Island notary renewal expired 30 days
articles.intent: Manage renewal timing, authority and personal records
articles.title: Rhode Island Renewal Gaps, the 30-Day Holdover and Permanent Notary IDs
articles.description: Distinguish a permanent notary ID from a limited commission term and plan accurate renewal records and tools.
articles.h1: A permanent ID does not make the commission permanent
articles.lede: Rhode Island keeps a notary's identification number through renewals and expired commissions. Authority still depends on the appointment, term and limited statutory holdover.

sections.heading: Preserve the existing ID
sections.body: The SOS renewal page states that the notary ID is permanent and never changes. Use it on a renewal even after the commission has expired. The number identifies the person's commission history, while the commission certificate supplies its operative dates. A completed renewal submitted before expiration preserves the month and day while changing the year. An incomplete submission can be returned and can affect that date continuity.

sections.heading: Apply the actual expiration rule
sections.body: Section 42-30.1-15(g) allows an appointed notary who is not reappointed to continue officiating for 30 days after expiration. The renewal page repeats the allowance and says to use the current commission's expiration date in the certificate. The provision does not create an unlimited extension while an application is pending. Once that period ends, await renewed authority before performing another act.

sections.heading: Keep the renewal file complete
sections.body: The renewal route again requires original form signatures and an oath before a Rhode Island notary, followed by physical submission and the ordinary $80 fee. The Department recommends reviewing the law, Standards and manual, attending training and aiming for 80% on the assessment. A missing page or an unsigned oath can delay processing. A purchase or training result is not the Department's reappointment.

sections.heading: Review tools and historical records
sections.body: The renewal page directs a notary to replace a stamp that is noncompliant or carries outdated information. A stamp displaying the previous expiration should be updated. Retain historical records according to the applicable duties and recommendations. The Standards recommend seven-year retention of an elected traditional journal after end-of-commission events, while section 12.1 separately imposes the default ten-year remote-recording period. Each record serves its own purpose.

faqs.q: Does a renewal receive a new notary ID?
faqs.a: The SOS says the original notary ID is permanent and should be reused.

faqs.q: May a notary act 45 days after expiration merely because renewal is pending?
faqs.a: The statutory holdover is 30 days. A pending application does not extend it beyond that period.
